# R tutorial 

## Packages used in this guide

Run the block below at the top of every script before working through these notes. The `pacman::p_load()` call will install any package that is not yet on your machine and then load all of them in one step.

```{r load-guide-packages, results='hide'}
if (!require(pacman)) install.packages("pacman")

pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,    # data wrangling and plotting (dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr, readr, ...)
  haven,        # read Stata .dta files
  labelled,     # work with value labels from Stata files
  survey,       # analyse complex survey data with design-based inference
  lmtest,       # robust standard errors for regression models
  sandwich,     # variance estimators that feed into lmtest
  car,          # test linear combinations of regression coefficients
  margins,      # compute predicted margins (average marginal effects)
  fastDummies,  # generate dummy variables from categorical columns
  modelsummary,
  questionr,
  texreg
)
```


### What each package does in this guide

| Package | What it is | What it does here |
|---|---|---|
| **tidyverse** | A bundle of packages (`dplyr`, `ggplot2`, `tidyr`, `readr`, and more) that share a consistent design | Used throughout for every day data tasks: filtering rows, creating new variables, summarising by group, reshaping data between wide and long formats, and producing all plots |
| **haven** | A reader for proprietary data formats | Loads the MICS `.dta` files produced in Stata into R with `read_dta()`, preserving value labels and variable labels so they are accessible in R |
| **labelled** | A toolkit for working with labelled data from survey files | Lets us inspect value labels (`val_labels()`), search variable names *and* labels at the same time (`look_for()`), and convert labelled integers to readable factors at the point of use rather than permanently |
| **survey** | A full survey-analysis toolkit | Defines the complex sampling design (clusters, strata, weights) with `svydesign()` so that all subsequent means, proportions, and regression models correctly account for the design — the R equivalent of Stata's `svyset` and `svy:` prefix |
| **lmtest** | Hypothesis testing tools for regression models | Used with `coeftest()` to apply cluster-robust standard errors to regression output, replacing the default standard errors that assume independence |
| **sandwich** | Sandwich variance estimators | Provides the `vcovCL()` estimator that `lmtest` uses to compute cluster-robust standard errors — the two packages are always used together |
| **car** | Companion to Applied Regression | Supplies `linearHypothesis()`, which tests any linear combination of regression coefficients — the R equivalent of Stata's `test` command, used here for interaction decomposition and joint significance tests |
| **margins** | Marginal effects for regression models | Computes predicted values and average marginal effects after a regression, producing results equivalent to Stata's `margins` command — particularly useful for interpreting interaction terms |
| **fastDummies** | Fast creation of dummy variables | Expands a categorical column into a set of 0/1 indicator variables with `dummy_cols()`, used in Module 3 for creating contract-teacher and baseline group indicators |

\newpage

# Getting to Know Your Data in R


**OBJECTIVES:** By the end of this lab, you should have:

- Gained skills in loading and exploring a dataset in R
- Learned to use key summarising and data-checking commands
- Prepared data for regression analysis

By this point you should have R and RStudio open and be comfortable running commands from a script. If you need a refresher on the RStudio interface, packages, or getting help, refer back to the **Getting Started with R** section above.

## 1. LOOKING AT SOME OF THE DATA, AND HOW IT IS CAPTURED IN R

You will need to download the data from MS Teams before you can open it in R. Unzip `mics6.zip` from the folder [Name of training] / MICS6 and save it somewhere convenient (e.g. your desktop or project folder).

Load the dataset by running the following, replacing the path with the location of your unzipped file:

```{r clear-reload, results='hide'}
rm(list = ls())          # removes all objects from memory
dat <- read_dta("./MICS6/ipums_mics6_africa.dta")
```

The `rm(list = ls())` line clears everything from memory before loading — the equivalent of Stata's `clear all`. In R, this is optional since assigning a new dataset to the same object name simply overwrites the old one, but it is good practice when re-running a script from scratch. Note that `read_dta()` is provided by the **haven** package, which was loaded earlier on in this guide. In practice, keeping a single script or R Markdown document that loads the data once at the top and then creates variables sequentially is good practice, exactly as you would structure a Stata do-file.

The dataset we are using is a harmonised version of several MICS surveys. MICS stands for the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey and is a household survey run by UNICEF in many different countries around the world with a focus on health and education outcomes. If you go to the MICS website (https://mics.unicef.org/) and navigate to the surveys tab, you will only find individual country datasets available for download. The dataset that you have now loaded into R was created for this course using Stata code from IPUMS (https://www.ipums.org/), a research unit that focuses on data harmonisation and integration. Specifically, the dataset was created using code from the IPUMS-MICS project (https://mics.ipums.org/mics/) that allows us to create a single dataset from many separate country datasets with variables that all have the same names and value codes (harmonised).

First let's take a more detailed look at what variables are stored in the data set. In R you can inspect structure and dimensions:

```{r describe, eval=FALSE}
# Structure: variable names, types, first values (like Stata's describe)
str(dat)
```


```{r glimpse, eval=FALSE}
# Or a compact summary (tidyverse style)
glimpse(dat)
```

You can see how many observations and variables there are:

```{r count, results='hide'}
# Number of rows (observations) – like Stata's count
nrow(dat)

# Number of columns (variables)
ncol(dat)
```

To view the data in a spreadsheet-like window (like Stata’s browse):

```{r browse, eval=FALSE}
View(dat)
```

You should note the following:

- Each **observation** (here, each child aged 5–17 in the household with recorded information) appears in a **row**. Moving across the row shows that child’s values for each variable. For example, the first person might live in Algeria, in 2018–9, in cluster 1, household number 7, and scrolling across you see she is a girl aged 14 living in an urban area.  
- Each **variable** appears in a **column**. What are the age and gender variables called?

Using the data viewer or subsetting, find the 420th observation. What is this child’s age? Their gender?

## 2. SIMPLE SUMMARISING COMMANDS

A frequency distribution table lists all the observed values for a given variable and the number of observations in each category. In R we use `table()` for one- and two-way frequency counts (similar to Stata’s `tabulate`). 

**A note on value labels.** When a dataset is read from a Stata `.dta` file using `haven::read_dta()`, variables are stored as **labelled integers** — the underlying values are numbers (e.g. 1, 2, 3 for countries) but they carry text labels (e.g. "Algeria", "Ghana"). In Stata you would toggle the display of these labels with `numlabel, add` or `numlabel, remove`. In R the idiomatic approach is different: **keep the variable as a numeric/integer for all data manipulation and calculations, and convert to a labelled factor only at the point where you need readable labels** — for example in a table or a plot. You can do this with `haven::as_factor()` inline. To inspect the code-to-label mapping for any variable, use `labelled::val_labels()`:

```{r labels-demo, results='hide'}
# Inspect the code-to-label mapping (like Stata's codebook or label list)
labelled::val_labels(dat$country)
```

```{r table, results='hide'}
# Human-readable frequency table (equivalent to tab country in Stata after numlabel, add)
table(as_factor(dat$country))
```

The use of `as_factor()` expands all value labels defined in the Stata file, including countries that exist in the label dictionary but have zero observations in the data, resulting in the bloated output you're seeing.To remove factor levels that have no observations, we can use `droplevels()`

```{r droplevels, results='hide'}
# Human-readable frequency table (equivalent to tab country in Stata after numlabel, add)
table(droplevels(as_factor(dat$country)))
```

How many observations are from Lesotho?

For help on any function, use `?functionname`, e.g. `?table`. The help page opens in the Help pane in RStudio. Unlike Stata’s help files which have clickable sub-entries (e.g. "tabulate oneway" vs "tabulate twoway"), R’s help pages cover all variants of a function in one page — scroll down to the **Arguments** and **Examples** sections, which are usually the most useful parts.

We can describe the time dimension of the dataset:

```{r tab-year, results='hide'}

table(dat$year)
```

Note that `as_factor()` is most useful for variables like `country` or `urban` where the underlying codes are arbitrary numbers that need labels to be interpretable. For variables like `year` where the numeric values are already self-explanatory, `table(dat$year)` directly gives a cleaner result. Where you do use `as_factor()`, wrapping it in `droplevels()` - as above - is good practice, it drops any factor levels that exist in the Stata label dictionary but have no observations in the data, preventing empty categories from cluttering your output.

For a two-way table of country and year:

```{r tab-country-year, results='hide'}
table(droplevels(as_factor(dat$country)), dat$year)
```

Which country appears more than once in our dataset? Consider another two-way table:

```{r tab-country-urban, results='hide'}
table(droplevels(as_factor(dat$country)), droplevels(as_factor(dat$urban)))

```

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=idocolor, colframe=datafirstteal, title=\textbf{BOX: TABLE WITH ROW, COL, CELL}]

Row percentages give the percentage of the ROW observations which are in each COLUMN category
(percentages across each row sum to 100). Column percentages give the percentage of the COLUMN
observations which are in each ROW category. Cell percentages give the percentage of the sample in each cell.

\medskip
The \texttt{table()} function gives raw counts. For \textbf{row percentages} (percentages within each row
that fall in each column), use \texttt{prop.table()} with \texttt{margin = 1}:

\begin{verbatim}
prop.table(table(dat$country, dat$urban), margin = 1) * 100
\end{verbatim}

So, for example, we might see that 67.63\% of learners from Algeria in our sample live in urban areas.

\medskip
For \textbf{column percentages} (percentages within each column that fall in each row):

\begin{verbatim}
prop.table(table(dat$country, dat$urban), margin = 2) * 100
\end{verbatim}

For \textbf{cell percentages} (percent of the whole sample in each cell):

\begin{verbatim}
prop.table(table(dat$country, dat$urban)) * 100
\end{verbatim}

E.g.\ 8.4\% of the sample might be Malawian learners from rural areas.

\medskip
To learn more, use \texttt{?table} and \texttt{?prop.table}.

\end{tcolorbox}

## 3. FINDING A UNIQUE IDENTIFIER

An important first step in getting to know your dataset is finding out the unit of analysis and what uniquely identifies observations. We saw there are 184,190 observations (or whatever `nrow(dat)` shows). It is important to know which variable or combination of variables uniquely identifies these observations and what each row represents (a person, a classroom, a school?). If we inspect the data again, the IPUMS-MICS approach usefully includes a variable called `unitanalysis`. In R:

```{r ta-unitanalysis, results='hide'}
table(droplevels(as_factor(dat$unitanalysis)))
```

This tells us that the unit of analysis in this dataset is children aged 5–17 years. Typically, datasets won’t include such a convenient variable. However, it is more normal for datasets to include some type of “ID” or “unique number” variable. We can check whether a combination of variables uniquely identifies rows. Some investigation of the IPUMS and MICS documentation suggested that the combination of `sample`, `hhno` and `linech` might uniquely identify each child.

To learn about these variables (similar to Stata’s `codebook`), inspect them. In Stata, `codebook` tells you the variable type, label, number of unique values, range, number of missing observations, and value labels all at once. In R we can get equivalent information using a combination of functions:

```{r codebook, results='hide'}
# Variable type and basic stats (like Stata's codebook for numeric variables)
summary(dat[, c("sample", "hhno", "linech")])

# Number of unique values per variable
sapply(dat[, c("sample", "hhno", "linech")], function(x) length(unique(x)))

# Value labels attached (if any) – useful for labelled variables from .dta files
labelled::val_labels(dat$sample)

# Number of missing values per variable
colSums(is.na(dat[, c("sample", "hhno", "linech")]))

# Number of unique combinations of the three variables:
nrow(unique(dat[, c("sample", "hhno", "linech")]))
```

How many samples are there? There are only 80 unique household numbers and 27 unique lines within households. These hardly seem enough to uniquely identify 180 thousand children, but that can be the case when we combine these variables.

Check whether the combination uniquely identifies rows (like Stata’s `isid`):

```{r isid, results='hide'}
nrow(dat) == nrow(unique(dat[, c("sample", "hhno", "linech")]))

# If FALSE, this combination is not unique. Try adding cluster:
nrow(dat) == nrow(unique(dat[, c("sample", "cluster", "hhno", "linech")]))
```

If the last line returns `TRUE`, that combination uniquely identifies the children. To make browsing easier, create a single unique identifier (like Stata’s `egen childid = group(sample cluster hhno linech)`):

```{r egen-childid, results='hide'}
library(dplyr)
# Modern dplyr equivalent of Stata's egen group():
dat <- dat %>%
  group_by(sample, cluster, hhno, linech) %>%
  mutate(childid = cur_group_id()) %>%
  ungroup()
nrow(dat) == length(unique(dat$childid))  # should be TRUE
```

Now confirm the new variable works as a unique identifier (like Stata's `codebook childid` and `isid childid`):

```{r unique-childid, results='hide'}
# How many unique values does childid have?
length(unique(dat$childid))
# Does it uniquely identify every row?
nrow(dat) == length(unique(dat$childid))   # should be TRUE
# Any missing values?
sum(is.na(dat$childid))                    # should be 0
```




When browsing, it is often easiest to have the unique identifier as the first column. Reorder columns:

```{r order, results='hide'}
dat <- dat %>% 
  select(childid, everything())
# Or: dat <- dat[, c("childid", setdiff(names(dat), "childid"))]

# names(dat) this confirms if childid is now the first column in the dataframe
```

Confirm with `names(dat)` and `View(dat)`.


## 4. EXAMINING VARIABLES

Often we are interested in whether a dataset contains a certain variable, and reading a long list of variables from `str()` or `glimpse()` can be tedious. In Stata you would use `lookfor`, which searches both **variable names and variable labels**. The direct R equivalent is `labelled::look_for()`, which does the same — searching both names and any labels that came with the `.dta` file. This matters because some variables have uninformative short names but descriptive labels, so searching only names would miss them.

Suppose you are interested in studying the effect of private schooling on numeracy scores. First find variables related to school type:

```{r lookfor-type, results='hide'}
# Searches both variable names AND variable labels (like Stata's lookfor)
look_for(dat, "type")

# Base R alternative (names only – misses label-only matches):
# names(dat)[grepl("type", names(dat), ignore.case = TRUE)]
```

You might see a variable called `schooltype`. Tabulate it:

```{r ta-schooltype, results='hide'}
table(as_factor(dat$schooltype))

```

Next, look for variables related to numeracy. Let’s first try “number”:

```{r lookfor-number, results='hide'}
look_for(dat, "number")
```

This brings up variables like `flbigger1` and `flnumadd1`. Do you notice that they all have “fl” in the prefix? A common practice by dataset processors is to use prefixes for variables in the same questionnaire module. This is a hint. Search more broadly:

```{r lookfor-fl, results='hide'}
look_for(dat, "fl")
```

Now we see a full range of assessment variables including numeracy items like `flrecognize1` that don’t contain the word “number” and would have been missed the first time around.

You might see variables like `flbigger1`, `flnumadd1`, etc. To view the unique identifier and a set of similarly named variables (like Stata’s browse with wildcards), select those columns:

```{r browse-numeracy, eval=FALSE}
dat %>%
  select(childid, matches("^flrecognize[1-5]$"),
         starts_with("flbigger"), 
         starts_with("flnumadd"), 
         starts_with("flnumseq")) %>%
  View()
```

In R, missing data are represented by `NA`. How did child 17502 do on the numeracy tests? Subset that row:

```{r browse-if, results='hide'}
flvars <- dat %>% 
  select(matches("^flrecognize[1-5]$"),
         starts_with("flbigger"),
         starts_with("flnumadd"),
         starts_with("flnumseq")) %>% 
  names()

dat %>% 
  filter(childid == 17502) %>% 
  select(childid, flvars)
```

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=idocolor, colframe=datafirstteal, title=\textbf{BOX: SUBSETTING IN R}]

In R we limit data to particular groups by \textbf{subsetting} (filtering) with logical conditions,
similar to Stata's \texttt{if}. Use comparison and logical operators:

\medskip
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
\textbf{Meaning} & \textbf{Stata} & \textbf{R} \\
\midrule
Equal            & \texttt{==}                             & \texttt{==}  \\
Not equal        & \texttt{\textasciitilde=} / \texttt{!=} & \texttt{!=}  \\
Greater than     & \texttt{>}                              & \texttt{>}   \\
Less than        & \texttt{<}                              & \texttt{<}   \\
Greater or equal & \texttt{>=}                             & \texttt{>=}  \\
Less or equal    & \texttt{<=}                             & \texttt{<=}  \\
Or               & \texttt{|}                              & \texttt{|}   \\
And              & \texttt{\&}                             & \texttt{\&}  \\
Not              & \texttt{\textasciitilde}                & \texttt{!}   \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\medskip

Example: one- and two-way tables for urban observations only:

\begin{verbatim}
table(dat$age, dat$sexfs)[, 1:2]   # example; for urban == 1:
dat_urban <- dat %>% filter(urban == 1)
table(dat_urban$age, dat_urban$sexfs)
prop.table(table(dat_urban$age, dat_urban$sexfs), margin = 2) * 100
\end{verbatim}

\textit{Practice:} What percentage of the sample from Algeria lives in urban areas?
What percentage of 15-year-old boys live in rural areas?
What percentage of the sample are girls living in Malawi?

\end{tcolorbox}


## 5. EXAMINING VARIABLES FURTHER

Suppose you are interested in the distribution of age for Grade 2. Search for variables related to age and grade, then focus on current grade:

```{r ta-edgradecurr, results='hide'}
table(droplevels(as_factor(dat$edgradecurr)))
```

A useful way to describe numeric data is summary statistics (like Stata’s `sum`):

```{r sum-age, results='hide'}
summary(dat$age)
mean(dat$age, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(dat$age, na.rm = TRUE)
```

What is the average age? The standard deviation? Limit to Grade 2:

```{r sum-age-grade2, results='hide'}
dat %>% 
  filter(edgradecurr == 2) %>% 
  summarise(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE), 
            sd_age = sd(age, na.rm = TRUE))
```

A table of age for Grade 2 shows the distribution more clearly:

```{r ta-age-grade2, results='hide'}
table(dat$age[dat$edgradecurr == 2])
```

Comparing the mean to the distribution: although the mean might be around 10 years, most Grade 2 children might cluster around 7 and 8. Why is the mean so much higher? Inspect with a histogram.

If you just type `hist(dat_g2$age)` without specifying breaks, R will choose its own bin width automatically — often something like 0.27 years, giving you many narrow, unevenly spaced bars that are hard to read. This is because R (like Stata by default) treats age as a generic continuous variable. But age recorded in whole years is a **discrete** variable: it increases in chunks of exactly 1. We should tell R to use bins of width 1 so that each bar represents exactly one year of age:

```{r results='hide'}
dat_g2 <- dat %>% filter(edgradecurr == 2)
```

```{r hist-age-grade2, eval=FALSE}
# Poor default (R picks bin width automatically, often a fraction of a year):
hist(dat_g2$age)

# Better: integer breaks so each bar = one year (like Stata's hist age, discrete)
hist(dat_g2$age,
     breaks = seq(min(dat_g2$age, na.rm = TRUE),
                  max(dat_g2$age, na.rm = TRUE) + 1) - 0.5,
     main = "Age in Grade 2", xlab = "Age", col = "steelblue")
```

The second plot is evenly spaced and each bin clearly represents one year of age. A continuous variable like income or a wealth index score could increase by fractions, so using the default bin width is appropriate there — but for discrete variables, always specify your own breaks.

Or with ggplot2:

```{r hist-ggplot, eval=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
dat %>% filter(edgradecurr == 2) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = 0.5, fill = "steelblue", col = "white") +
  labs(title = "Age in Grade 2", x = "Age")
```

You might see heaping at 7–8 and again at older ages (bimodal). Does it seem right that there are so many 12–17 year-olds in Grade 2? Check by country (like Stata’s `by()`):

```{r hist-by-country, eval=FALSE}
dat %>% filter(edgradecurr == 2) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ as_factor(country)) +
  labs(title = "Age in Grade 2 by country")

```

And by grade (restricting to non-missing grade, e.g. `edgradecurr < 96`):

```{r hist-by-grade, eval=FALSE}
dat %>% filter(edgradecurr < 96) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ edgradecurr) +
  labs(title = "Age by current grade")
```

The bimodal shape may be more prominent in earlier grades. From the MICS questionnaire, education level and grade are both relevant; the variable `edlevelcurr` is needed. Compare level and grade:

```{r ta-grade, results='hide'}
table(dat$edlevelcurr)
```

```{r, ta-level-grade, results='hide'}
table(droplevels(as_factor(dat$edlevelcurr)), dat$edgradecurr)
```

To focus on “primary” Grade 2 (e.g. level 200), plot age:

```{r hist-grade2-primary, eval=FALSE}
dat %>% filter(edgradecurr == 2, edlevelcurr == 200) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = 0.5, fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Age in Grade 2 (primary level)")
```

This can give a clearer bell-shaped distribution. This exercise illustrates the usefulness of inspecting distributions and checking questionnaires.


## 6. QUICK INTRODUCTION TO R SCRIPTS AND R MARKDOWN

In R you can type commands in the Console, but for reproducibility we use **scripts** (.R) or **R Markdown** (.Rmd) documents. We will focus on using R scripts in this guide. An R script is a sequence of commands that you can run line by line or as a whole.

Example of a short script (like a Stata do-file):

```{r do-file-example, eval=FALSE}
# Clear environment (optional; like Stata's clear all)
# rm(list = ls())

dat2 <- read_dta("./MICS6/ipums_mics6_africa.dta")
table(dat2$country, dat2$urban)
```

Save your script (e.g. `example.R`) and run it from the Console with `source("example.R")`. If you create new variables in the same script and run it again, you are re-running from the top; if you reload the data, new variables are created again. Keeping a single script that loads data once and then creates variables is good practice.

## 7. MISSING DATA CODES

Returning to the research question about private school and numeracy scores: inspect `schooltype`:

```{r ta-schooltype-missing, results='hide'}
table(dat$schooltype, useNA = "ifany")
```

Value code 10 = Government/public, 20 = Religious/faith, 30 = Private. Codes 97–99 may be Don’t know, Missing, NIU. If you run `mean(dat$schooltype, na.rm = TRUE)` you get a number that is not interpretable like a mean of age, because `schooltype` is **categorical**.

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=idocolor, colframe=datafirstteal, title=\textbf{BOX: TYPES OF VARIABLES}]

Let's take a moment to review different types of variables. The statistical and graphical tools
used to understand the distributions of the various types of variables are quite different, so it
is important to understand the differences between these measures.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Continuous variables} have an infinite number of possible values between any two
    observed values (e.g.\ age in principle, or wealth index score). They can be truly continuous
    (income, price) or \textbf{discrete} (age in years).
  \item \textbf{Categorical variables} are made up of distinct categories; the numeric codes are
    arbitrary (e.g.\ school type, home language, gender). You should not interpret the mean of a
    categorical variable.
  \item \textbf{Ordinal categorical} variables have a meaningful order (e.g.\ age group) but the
    mean of the code is still not interpretable.
  \item \textbf{Dummy (indicator) variables} take only 0 and 1. The \textbf{mean} of a dummy is
    the \textbf{proportion} (share) in the category coded 1.
\end{itemize}

\medskip
Look at the frequency table again and think about missing data. Generally we would call codes 10--52
``non-missing and say something like 69.27\% of the sample have non-missing 	exttt{schooltype}.
But there are different types of missing: non-response (e.g.\ 97), unspecified missing (98), and
NIU (not in universe, e.g.\ 99). The \texttt{table(\ldots, useNA = "ifany")} shows how many have
\texttt{NA} in R (Statas ``.).
To include all missings in the table:

\begin{verbatim}
table(dat$schooltype, useNA = "ifany")
\end{verbatim}

NIU might apply when the question was not asked (e.g.\ foundational learning module only for
children 7--14; or skip patterns). It is important to understand who has non-missing vs missing
data. Investigate using the questionnaire and cross-tabs, e.g.\ school type by current school attendance:

\begin{verbatim}
table(dat$schooltype, dat$schoolcurr, useNA = "ifany")
\end{verbatim}

And by ever attended school:

\begin{verbatim}
table(dat$schooltype, dat$schoolever, useNA = "ifany")
\end{verbatim}

Limit to children who ever attended and currently attend, and exclude ECE
(e.g.\ \texttt{edlevelcurr != 100}):

\begin{verbatim}
dat_eligible <- dat %>% filter(schoolever == 1, schoolcurr == 1, edlevelcurr != 100)
table(dat_eligible$schooltype, useNA = "ifany")
\end{verbatim}

Check whether missing \texttt{schooltype} is concentrated in certain countries:

\begin{verbatim}
dat %>% filter(is.na(schooltype)) %>% count(country)
table(dat$country[is.na(dat$schooltype)])
\end{verbatim}

If only a few countries have all missing for this question, that is useful to note.

\end{tcolorbox}

## 8. CREATING NEW VARIABLES

Create a “clean” dummy for private school (1 = private, 0 = non-private, and set true missings to `NA`). In R we use `mutate()` and `case_when()` or `ifelse()` (similar to Stata’s `generate` and `replace`):

```{r gen-private, results='hide'}
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(
    private = case_when(
      schooltype == 30 ~ 1L,
      schooltype %in% c(10, 20, 50, 52) ~ 0L,
      schooltype >= 97 | is.na(schooltype) ~ NA_integer_
    )
  )
table(dat$schooltype, dat$private, useNA = "ifany")
```

Shortcut: a dummy that is 1 when `schooltype == 30` and 0 otherwise (with missings from schooltype >= 97 set to NA as above):

```{r gen-private-short, results='hide'}
dat <- dat %>% 
  mutate(private = ifelse(schooltype == 30, 1L, 
                          ifelse(schooltype >= 97 | is.na(schooltype), 
                                 NA_integer_, 0L)))
```

Or using a single recode-style step (like Stata’s `recode`):

```{r recode-private, results='hide'}
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(private = case_when(
    schooltype %in% c(10, 20, 50, 52) ~ 0,
    schooltype == 30 ~ 1,
    schooltype >= 97 ~ NA_real_,
    TRUE ~ NA_real_
  ))
```

Confirm with a two-way table. The mean of `private` (excluding NA) is the share in private school:

```{r su-private, results='hide'}
mean(dat$private, na.rm = TRUE)
```

**A note on labelling in R vs Stata.** In Stata, labelling is done upfront as a standard setup step: `la var private "Attends a private school"` gives the variable a label, and `lab define` / `lab val` assign text to the numeric codes (0 = "Non-private", 1 = "Private"). These labels then travel with the variable everywhere.

In R this is not standard practice, and for good reason: converting a numeric column to a **factor** — R's closest equivalent to a value-labelled variable — permanently changes how R treats it. Factor columns behave differently in models (they generate dummy variables automatically), in arithmetic (you cannot add factors), and in many other functions. Converting prematurely can cause unexpected behaviour downstream.

The idiomatic R approach is to **keep the column numeric and convert to a factor at the point of use** — in a model formula, a table, or a plot — rather than mutating the column in the data frame itself:

```{r label-private, results='hide'}
# Keep 'private' as numeric in the data frame (safe for calculations and models)

# Convert to factor inline when you need labels in a table:
table(factor(dat$private, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Non-private", "Private")))
```

```{r bar-private, eval=FALSE}
# Or in a ggplot:
ggplot(dat, aes(x = factor(private, labels = c("Non-private", "Private")))) +
  geom_bar() + labs(x = "School type")

# In a model formula, also convert inline if you want R to treat it as categorical:
# svyglm(numscore ~ factor(private) + age, design = svy_des)
```

You can store a metadata note about the variable using `comment()` if it helps you remember the coding:

```{r comment-private, results='hide'}
comment(dat$private) <- "1 = Private school, 0 = Non-private (public/religious/other)"
comment(dat$private)   # retrieve the note
```

This keeps the column numeric while giving you a portable reminder of what the codes mean.

## 9. EXTENSIONS TO CREATING NEW VARIABLES

Suppose we want a numeracy score by summing 20 item dummies. First inspect one component’s codes:

```{r ta-flbigger1, results='hide'}
table(dat$flbigger1)
```

Decide which codes count as correct (1), wrong (0), or missing. For each item we can create a clean dummy (1 = correct, 0 = incorrect, NA = missing/NIU). Doing this for many similarly named variables is easier with a loop or with `across()` in dplyr. Example for one set (flrecognize1–5), using a loop in R:

```{r loop-clean, results='hide'}
stems <- c("flrecognize", "flbigger", "flnumadd", "flnumseq")

for (stem in stems) {
  for (y in 1:5) {
    var_orig <- paste0(stem, y)
    var_new  <- paste0(stem, y, "_clean")
    dat[[var_new]] <- ifelse(dat[[var_orig]] == 1, 1L,
                      ifelse(dat[[var_orig]] >= 8, NA_integer_, 0L))
  }
}
# Similarly for flbigger, flnumadd, flnumseq...
```

Then sum the 20 clean components (either by listing them or by selecting columns that end with `_clean` and using `rowSums`). Be careful: if any component is NA, do you want the total score to be NA (complete case) or the sum of non-missing items? For a strict “complete case” score:

```{r numscore, results='hide'}
clean_vars <- c(paste0("flrecognize", 1:5, "_clean"), paste0("flbigger", 1:5, "_clean"),
                paste0("flnumadd", 1:5, "_clean"), paste0("flnumseq", 1:5, "_clean"))
dat$numscore <- rowSums(dat[, clean_vars], na.rm = FALSE)  # NA if any missing
# With na.rm = TRUE you get sum of non-missing (like egen rowtotal, missing in Stata)
summary(dat$numscore)
```

Only children aged 7–14 with consent might have taken the test. Tabulate with a filter:

```{r ta-numscore-eligible, results='hide'}
dat %>% 
  filter(age >= 7, 
         age <= 14,
         flconsent == 1,
         flassentchild == 1) %>%
  count(numscore)  # or table(..., useNA = "ifany")
```

Using `rowSums(..., na.rm = TRUE)` gives a score that ignores missing items (like Stata’s `egen rowtotal(..., missing)`); a child with 15 correct and 5 missing would get 15. The complete-case approach (NA if any item missing) is often preferred. You can count how many items are missing per child with `rowSums(is.na(dat[, clean_vars]))`.

## 10. USING COMPLEX SURVEY DATA: THE SURVEY PACKAGE

When we want **inferential** statistics (standard errors, confidence intervals) that reflect the sampling design, we use the **survey** package in R (analogous to Stata’s `svy` suite). First we define a survey design with `svydesign()`, then we use survey-aware functions like `svymean()`.

Define the design (cluster, strata, weights). Variable names below match the Stata example; adjust to your dataset:

```{r svyset-cluster, results='hide'}
library(survey)
svy_des_cluster <- svydesign(
  ids = ~ imicscluster,
 # strata = ~ urban,
 # weights = ~ weightfs,
  data = dat,
 nested = TRUE
)
```

Estimate means (like Stata’s `svy: mean`):

```{r svy-mean, results='hide'}
svymean(~ numscore + wscore, svy_des_cluster, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Design effects (DEFF) can be computed by comparing variance under the complex design to variance under simple random sampling. R’s survey package computes this with `svymean()` plus the `deff = TRUE` argument:

```{r deff, results='hide'}
# Estimate mean with design effect (like Stata's svy: mean + estat effects, deff)
svymean(~ numscore + wscore, svy_des_cluster, deff = "replace", na.rm = TRUE)
```

The DEFF tells you how many more observations you would need under simple random sampling (SRS) to achieve the same precision. For example, if `wscore` has a DEFF of 6.57 and your complex sample has 95,833 observations, your design is only as precise as an SRS of 95,833 / 6.57 = **14,586 observations**. Can you calculate and interpret the DEFF for `numscore`?

Why might the DEFF be higher for `wscore` than `numscore`? Household wealth varies at the household level and will be the same for all children in the same household. Children in the same cluster are also likely to have similar wealth levels. This makes wealth more homogeneous within clusters than numeracy scores, which vary at the child level. 

We can measure this directly using the intra-cluster correlation (ICC), which captures how similar observations are within clusters — the R equivalent of Stata's loneway. Computing the ICC formally requires fitting a random effects model, which is computationally slow on a dataset this large. A fast and interpretable approximation is to compare the variance of cluster means to the total variance:



```{r icc, results='hide'}
library(lme4)

# For wscore
model_ws <- lmer(wscore ~ 1 + (1 | imicscluster), data = dat, REML = TRUE)
icc_wscore <- as.numeric(VarCorr(model_ws)$imicscluster) / 
              (as.numeric(VarCorr(model_ws)$imicscluster) + sigma(model_ws)^2)

# For numscore
model_ns <- lmer(numscore ~ 1 + (1 | imicscluster), data = dat, REML = TRUE)
icc_numscore <- as.numeric(VarCorr(model_ns)$imicscluster) / 
                (as.numeric(VarCorr(model_ns)$imicscluster) + sigma(model_ns)^2)

icc_wscore
icc_numscore
```


The ICC should be notably higher for wscore than numscore, explaining the larger DEFF for wealth. Intuitively, the ICC measures how much of the total variation in a variable exists between clusters rather than within them — a high ICC means children in the same cluster are very similar on that variable, so each additional observation from the same cluster adds less new information than it would under simple random sampling.

```{r svyset_strata, results='hide'}
library(survey)
svy_des_strata <- svydesign(
 ids = ~ 1, # no clustering
 strata = ~ urban,
 # weights = ~ weightfs,
  data = dat,
 nested = TRUE
)
```


```{r svy-mean-strata, results='hide'}
svymean(~ numscore + wscore, svy_des_strata, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r deff-strata, results='hide'}
# Estimate mean with design effect (like Stata's svy: mean + estat effects, deff)
svymean(~ numscore + wscore, svy_des_strata, deff = "replace", na.rm = TRUE)
```

---

## 11. WEIGHTS

Weights are factors assigned to observations during post-processing of a survey. They serve several roles: accounting for unequal probability of selection (some people were more likely to be sampled than others), correcting for unit non-response, and calibration (ensuring the dataset reflects known population totals from an external benchmark such as a census). Crucially, incorporating weights changes the *point estimate* of statistics, not just the standard errors — this is the key difference from strata, which affect precision only.

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=idocolor, colframe=datafirstteal, title=\textbf{BOX: TYPES OF WEIGHTS (R / SURVEY)}]

\medskip
R and the \texttt{survey} package distinguish four weight types, mirroring Stata's \texttt{fweight}, \texttt{aweight}, \texttt{pweight}, and \texttt{iweight}:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Probability weights (pweights)} --- sampling weights: the inverse of the inclusion probability. A pweight of 30 means this observation had a 1-in-30 chance of selection and \textit{represents} 30 people in the population. Use these for survey inference. In \texttt{svydesign()}, the \texttt{weights} argument takes pweights.
  \item \textbf{Frequency weights (fweights)} --- represent the number of duplicated observations; must be integers. A fweight of 30 means there are 30 observations with identical values on all variables. Used for grouped data.
  \item \textbf{Analytic weights (aweights)} --- inversely proportional to the variance of an observation. Commonly used when observations are group averages and the weight is the group size. Stata rescales these to sum to 1; only relative weights matter.
  \item \textbf{Importance weights (iweights)} --- mostly used by programmers; not standard for survey inference.
\end{itemize}

\medskip
\textbf{Using the wrong weight type produces misleading standard errors.} The point estimate of the mean is the same whether you use analytic or probability weights, but the standard error is not. Always use pweights (via \texttt{svydesign()}) for survey inference.

\medskip
For MICS, use the person-level sampling weight \texttt{weightfs} as a pweight inside \texttt{svydesign()}.

\end{tcolorbox}

**Weights in practice: comparing approaches**

To see concretely how weights affect results, compare the unweighted mean, a simple weighted mean, and the full survey-design mean:

```{r weights-compare, results='hide'}
# Unweighted mean — sample statistic, treats all obs equally
mean(dat$numscore, na.rm = TRUE)

# Weighted mean — correct point estimate, but SE ignores clustering/stratification
weighted.mean(dat$numscore, dat$weightfs, na.rm = TRUE)

```

```{r}
dat %>%
  group_by(country= as_factor(country)) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_wscore = weighted.mean(wscore, w = weightfs, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_wscore   = sqrt(sum(weightfs * (wscore - weighted.mean(wscore, weightfs, na.rm = TRUE))^2, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(weightfs, na.rm = TRUE)),
    freq        = sum(weightfs, na.rm = TRUE),
    obs         = n()
  )
```
```{r}

# Frequency weights (fw) - integer counts
weighted.mean(dat$numscore, w = dat$weightfs, na.rm = TRUE)  # fw and aw give same point estimate

# Analytic weights (aw) - same point estimate as fw
weighted.mean(dat$numscore, w = dat$weightfs, na.rm = TRUE)

# Importance/probability weights (pw) - use survey package
svy_pw <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~weightfs, data = dat)
svymean(~numscore, svy_pw, na.rm = TRUE)

# Inverse weights (iw) - same point estimate as aw/fw
weighted.mean(dat$numscore, w = dat$weightfs, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r svyset_full, results='hide'}
library(survey)
svy_des_full <- svydesign(
 ids = ~ imicscluster,
 strata = ~ urban,
 weights = ~ weightfs,
  data = dat,
 nested = TRUE
)
```


```{r}
# Full survey-design mean — correct point estimate AND correct SE
svymean(~ numscore, svy_des_full, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The unweighted and weighted means will differ because weights correct for over- or under-representation of certain groups in the sample. The `weighted.mean()` and `svymean()` point estimates will match, but `svymean()` also accounts for clustering and stratification in its standard error — `weighted.mean()` does not. The wrong weight type is like Stata's `mean numscore [fw=weightfs]` — it produces an error or wrong SEs because frequency weights must be integers and are not meaningful here.

**Raising weights vs normalised weights**

Not all probability weights are *raising weights*. Raising weights sum to the population total, so you can use them to estimate population counts. Normalised weights are rescaled to sum to the sample size; they yield nationally representative proportions and means but not totals. Always check what your weight variable is designed to do — the survey documentation will say. For MICS, `weightfs` is a raising weight designed to recover nationally representative proportions and population totals.


## 12. DESCRIBING DATA: PLOTS AND TABLES

Describe your analysis sample (e.g. non-missing `numscore` and `private`, age 7–14):

```{r mysample, results='hide'}
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(mysample = !is.na(numscore) & 
           !is.na(private) &
           age >= 7 &
           age <= 14)

table(dat$mysample)
```

You can then restrict to the analysis sample for all subsequent commands, or subset once:

```{r keep-mysample, results='hide'}
dat_analysis <- dat %>%
  filter(mysample == 1)

nrow(dat_analysis)
```

For a histogram of `numscore` (discrete 0–20), base R or ggplot2:

```{r hist-numscore, results='hide'}
hist(dat_analysis$numscore, breaks = 0:21 - 0.5, main = "Numeracy score", xlab = "Score", col = "steelblue")
```

Weighted kernel density (conceptually like Stata’s `kdensity [aw=weightfs]`) can be done with `density(..., weights = ...)` or with the survey package. For a simple weighted density:

```{r kdensity, results='hide'}
d <- density(dat_analysis$numscore, weights = dat_analysis$weightfs / mean(dat_analysis$weightfs, na.rm = TRUE), na.rm = TRUE)
plot(d, main = "Numeracy score (weighted)")
```

Side-by-side densities by private school:

```{r kdensity-by-private, eval=FALSE}
dat_analysis %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = numscore, weight = weightfs, colour = factor(private))) +
  geom_density(bw = 1) +
  labs(title = "Numeracy score by private school", colour = "Private")
```

Or faceted:

```{r kdensity-facet, eval=FALSE}
dat_analysis %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = numscore, weight = weightfs)) +
  geom_density(bw = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ private, labeller = as_labeller(c("0" = "Non-private", "1" = "Private")))
```

For a bar chart of mean private by country (weighted), use the survey object or aggregate first:

```{r gr-bar, eval=FALSE}
dat_analysis %>%
  mutate(country = as_factor(country)) %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(mean_private = weighted.mean(private, weightfs, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(country, mean_private), y = mean_private)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Country", y = "Share in private school")
```

Descriptive table by private school (mean numscore, mean urban dummy, mean wealth, etc.): use `group_by(private)` and `summarise()`, or `tapply()` with `weighted.mean`. For mother’s education (categorical), report proportions by group; ensure sample size is consistent across rows (same analysis sample).
